info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 7.3: AI-Assisted Variant Classification and Adjudication.

questiontext.text: What is the central methodological question explored when applying language models to variant classification and collation?

generalfeedback.text: The test is whether semantic capability supplies what character-based alignment cannot, and whether it costs the reproducibility a critical apparatus requires.

answer.text: Whether semantic understanding can classify variants and recognize synonyms where character alignment fails, and whether it sacrifices the mathematical reproducibility required for an apparatus.

feedback.text: Correct. Language models navigate semantic proximity and taxonomy tiers, but their generative stochastic nature lacks the strict determinism of sequence alignment algorithms.

answer.text: Whether neural networks can physically restore damaged parchment fibers using laser printers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital methods analyze digitized text and images; they do not physically alter physical artifacts.

answer.text: Whether classical Greek manuscripts can be permanently deleted from university library servers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital humanities enhances access to historical manuscripts, not deletion.

answer.text: Whether Python should be completely replaced by assembly language for all textual scholarship.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Python remains the primary language for textual data science and collation pipelines.

questiontext.text: Why must classification, semantic identification, and adjudication be evaluated separately when testing AI models on collation data?

generalfeedback.text: Classification, semantic identification, and adjudication are three tasks with rising risk — evaluate them separately rather than reaching one verdict.

answer.text: They have distinctly different risk profiles: classification works on a fixed list, semantic identification risks hallucinations, and adjudication requires external evidence the model lacks.

feedback.text: Correct. Conflating these three tasks into a single score obscures where the model is helpful (classification) and where it is hazardous (unsupported adjudication).

answer.text: Because each task must be run on a completely different computer operating system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All tasks run within standard environments; separating them is an analytical and risk management necessity.

answer.text: Because TEI XML schemas only allow one prompt per academic semester.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI encodes markup structure, not prompt frequencies.

answer.text: Because the Gothenburg Model requires three separate commercial subscriptions to execute.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Gothenburg Model is an open conceptual architecture, not a commercial tool suite.

questiontext.text: Why is executing the identical prompt twice on the identical input an essential control when evaluating language models for critical apparatus production?

generalfeedback.text: Run the identical prompt twice and report the disagreement rate — for an apparatus, instability matters more than accuracy.

answer.text: It directly measures output instability and stochastic disagreement, testing whether the model meets the strict reproducibility demanded of scholarly claims.

feedback.text: Correct. If an apparatus changes every time the pipeline is re-run, it cannot serve as a stable foundation for scholarly citation and debate.

answer.text: It doubles the token processing fee to ensure high priority in GPU queues.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The repeat run is a scientific control for reproducibility, not a queue priority mechanism.

answer.text: It automatically clears the computer's temporary cache of obsolete Unicode fonts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Font caches are managed by the operating system, not prompt executions.

answer.text: It enables the model to translate Greek text into Latin on the second pass.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both passes use the same prompt instructions and input data.

questiontext.text: In the structured classification prompt, what is the specific analytical purpose of requiring the model to return same_lexeme: true|false?

generalfeedback.text: Asking whether two readings are forms of one lexeme forces the distinction between the morphological and lexical tiers into the open.

answer.text: It forces the model to make explicit whether two readings represent grammatical inflections of one word or two distinct vocabulary items, separating the morphological and lexical tiers.

feedback.text: Correct. Morphological variants (same lexeme) and lexical substitutions (different lexemes) carry very different stemmatic values; this field brings the underlying linguistic claim into the open.

answer.text: It forces the model to check whether both words have the exact same number of letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lexeme identity is a grammatical and lexical concept, not a character count.

answer.text: It commands the model to translate both words into modern German dialect.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The classification focuses on ancient Greek lemma identity.

answer.text: It allows the model to bypass Unicode normalization rules during tokenization.

feedback.text: Incorrect. same_lexeme is a JSON output field evaluating morphological relationships.

questiontext.text: When an editor and a language model disagree on whether a variant is morphological or lexical, how should the disagreement be resolved?

generalfeedback.text: Morphological versus lexical is where disagreement concentrates and where genealogical stakes are highest — resolve it with a lexicon, not by defaulting to your own answer.

answer.text: By consulting an authoritative Greek lexicon (such as LSJ or BDAG) to determine whether the two forms share a root lexeme, rather than defaulting to human intuition.

feedback.text: Correct. The morphological-versus-lexical boundary is a precise linguistic question where reference lexicons provide authoritative ground truth.

answer.text: By accepting whichever answer was generated in fewer milliseconds by the GPU.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Processing speed has no bearing on philological accuracy.

answer.text: By deleting the variant site from both manuscript witnesses entirely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Variant sites are preserved; their classification determines apparatus filtering.

answer.text: By flipping a coin to maintain mathematical neutrality between human and machine.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly decisions must be grounded in philological evidence.

questiontext.text: When asking a language model to identify semantic variants that character-based alignment missed, what constitutes the most serious failure mode?

generalfeedback.text: Verify every reported variant against the witness texts — a variant reported where both witnesses agree is a hallucination, the most serious failure here.

answer.text: A hallucinated variant where the model reports a substantive divergence at a location where both manuscript witnesses read identically.

feedback.text: Correct. Inventing non-existent differences corrupts the textual record and forces the editor to expend time verifying phantom readings.

answer.text: The model formatting its response as valid JSON instead of plain Markdown text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Valid JSON is the desired structured format for automated parsing.

answer.text: The model accurately identifying a synonym substitution in line 12.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Finding real synonym substitutions is the primary successful capability of semantic models.

answer.text: The model taking more than five seconds to process thirty lines of Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Latency is a minor performance detail compared to textual hallucinations.

questiontext.text: Why does a semantic identification method that yields two genuine finds alongside three hallucinations fail to save editorial labour?

generalfeedback.text: A method producing two genuine finds and three hallucinations saves no labour, because verifying the hallucinations requires the manual comparison it was meant to replace.

answer.text: Because every reported site must be manually audited against the facsimiles, so verifying false positives consumes the time saved by the genuine finds.

feedback.text: Correct. A tool with high hallucination rates creates manual audit overhead that negates its efficiency gains.

answer.text: Because hallucinations permanently damage the physical hard disk sectors of the server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hallucinations are invalid text outputs, not physical hardware damage.

answer.text: Because academic publishers charge monetary fines for every hallucinated variant found in peer review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The cost is editorial labour and lost reliability, not publisher fines.

answer.text: Because dynamic programming matrices refuse to load files that contain more than one error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alignment algorithms process any valid token list.

name.text: 08 Question: Task Three: The Transposition Test

questiontext.text: Why is a language model capable of recognizing a transposition as a single event when CollateX's core algorithm cannot?

generalfeedback.text: Recognizing a transposition as one event is where a model overcomes a limitation built into the graph model itself — construct a test if your witnesses do not supply one.

answer.text: The model reasons over global semantic relationships across the text rather than traversing a directed acyclic graph constrained by strict linear reading order.

feedback.text: Correct. CollateX's DAG strictly prohibits backward edges to prevent infinite loops, whereas a model evaluates meaning across disparate sentence positions.

answer.text: The model has access to the physical original autograph written by the ancient author.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Autographs do not survive; models operate on the transcribed text supplied in the prompt.

answer.text: The model converts the entire Greek alphabet into binary ASCII bits before comparing words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Binary conversion does not explain semantic transposition recognition.

answer.text: CollateX was intentionally programmed to ignore transpositions to save memory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The limitation is an inherent topological constraint of acyclic graphs.

name.text: 09 Question: Task Four: Adjudication, and Its Limits

questiontext.text: Why is an AI model's adjudication of which reading is original fundamentally untrustworthy when it asserts that a witness is 'of an earlier, superior textual family'?

generalfeedback.text: A model can apply internal criteria and cannot weigh witnesses — an adjudication citing external evidence you did not supply is fabricated.

answer.text: The model has no access to external codicological or stemmatic evidence and has fabricated a historical claim to justify its internal textual preference.

feedback.text: Correct. Models can weigh internal criteria (such as lectio difficilior), but claims about external witness reliability without supplied data are ungrounded fabrications.

answer.text: Because language models are programmed to only favor 16th-century printed editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models have no programmed bias toward specific centuries; they generate text based on prompts.

answer.text: Because Greek grammar prohibits any manuscript from being older than the 9th century CE.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many papyri and uncials date from the 2nd to 5th centuries CE.

answer.text: Because external genealogical evidence can only be calculated using quantum computers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. External evidence is historical, codicological, and stemmatic data gathered by scholars.

questiontext.text: What is indicated when repeat runs of a classification prompt yield the exact same variant tiers but cite completely different rationales?

generalfeedback.text: A model reaching the same conclusion by different reasoning is reproducible in its claims and not in its argument — an odd position for an apparatus.

answer.text: The model is substantively reproducible in its output claims but unstable in its underlying reasoning process.

feedback.text: Correct. While the final classification matches, differing arguments highlight the stochastic, non-deterministic nature of generative text generation.

answer.text: The model has achieved human-level philosophical consciousness.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generative models sample token probabilities; differing rationales reflect stochastic sampling variance.

answer.text: The Python JSON parser has corrupted the file encoding during serialization.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Serialization preserves strings; the difference originates in model generation.

answer.text: The Greek manuscript text has physically changed on disk between runs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The source text remains completely static across runs.

questiontext.text: What is the central opposition revealed when comparing Manual, CollateX, and Language Model collation methods?

generalfeedback.text: The method that can classify cannot be reproduced, and the method that is exactly reproducible cannot classify — that opposition is the week's finding.

answer.text: The method that can classify variants by significance cannot be deterministically reproduced, and the method that is strictly reproducible cannot classify.

feedback.text: Correct. CollateX aligns perfectly and reproducibly but lacks semantic classification; models classify semantically but lack determinism and transparency.

answer.text: Manual collation is completely free, while computational collation costs millions of dollars per page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Open-source tools like CollateX run with negligible computational cost on standard hardware.

answer.text: Language models can only process Latin texts, while CollateX can only process Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both tools handle multilingual corpora and multiple scripts cleanly.

answer.text: Manual collation produces perfect stemmatic trees without requiring editorial review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual work is prone to human fatigue and still requires rigorous verification.

name.text: 12 Question: Where the Model Genuinely Helps

questiontext.text: Under what workflow conditions is language model assistance both effective and methodologically safe in critical editing?

generalfeedback.text: Use the model for classification, where errors are checkable against a fixed list — never for the baseline alignment, which is already exact and reproducible.

answer.text: Classifying already established variant sites from a fixed list, where possible misclassifications are easily reviewed and verified against the readings.

feedback.text: Correct. Working from fixed CollateX sites prevents hallucinations and speeds up the bottleneck of sorting variants into taxonomy tiers for apparatus filtering.

answer.text: Generating the primary baseline alignment from raw un-normalized witness texts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Baseline alignment must be exact, transparent, and reproducible, which deterministic tools provide.

answer.text: Adjudicating theological disputes in biblical texts without human editorial oversight.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Adjudication requires deep historical, external, and theological judgement.

answer.text: Writing the entire edition introduction without referencing manuscript shelfmarks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Introductions require precise historical and codicological documentation.

questiontext.text: Why should the between-run disagreement rate of language model classifications be recorded as a Git commit trailer (e.g. Run-Disagreement: 3 of 34)?

generalfeedback.text: Record the between-run disagreement rate as a commit trailer — it belongs in the queryable history alongside the other provenance.

answer.text: It embeds the empirical stability and reproducibility measurement directly in the permanent, queryable history of the repository alongside other provenance metadata.

feedback.text: Correct. Documenting reproducibility metrics in commit trailers ensures that the reliability of AI-assisted steps is auditable by future scholars.

answer.text: It automatically triggers an automated email to the author of the language model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git trailers are local metadata fields used by repository tools and scholars.

answer.text: It is required by the Linux kernel compiler before building C programs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git trailers are convention-based metadata for version control history.

answer.text: It prevents other users from viewing the Git commit history without a password.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commit trailers are open, readable plain text metadata.

questiontext.text: Why must every model-reported semantic variant be verified against the actual witness transcriptions before being accepted?

generalfeedback.text: Verify every model-reported variant against the witness texts — that check is what separates a contribution from a hallucination.

answer.text: Verification is the sole mechanism that separates genuine synonym substitutions from hallucinated non-existent variants.

feedback.text: Correct. Because language models can invent differences where texts agree, unverified reports must never enter a scholarly edition.

answer.text: Verification converts the TEI XML file into an uncompressed binary executable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Verification is an editorial quality check, not binary compilation.

answer.text: Unverified variants will cause CollateX to delete all existing Git tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX does not manipulate Git repository tags.

answer.text: The W3C consortium conducts random audits of student repositories every Friday.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Verification is a philological responsibility, not an external compliance audit.

questiontext.text: When encountering a hallucinated variant or a fabricated claim about witness reliability, why should the student report it rather than quietly fixing it?

generalfeedback.text: Hallucinated variants and fabricated witness claims are findings to report, not problems to quietly clean up.

answer.text: Because hallucinations and fabrications are empirical findings about the methodology's capabilities and risk profile that belong in the scholarly assessment.

feedback.text: Correct. Suppressing failures discards the primary evidence needed to assess the limits of generative AI in critical editing.

answer.text: Because reporting failures qualifies the student for a cash reward from the AI vendor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The report is an academic assessment of methodology, not a vendor bug bounty.

answer.text: Because the TEI validator crashes if an error is corrected without a formal ticket.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI schemas validate markup structure, not documentation logs.

answer.text: Because fabricated claims become legally binding if not submitted within 24 hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly documentation records empirical results honestly.

name.text: 16 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: Why is measuring stability across repeat runs more critical than simply calculating raw accuracy when evaluating AI collation tools?

generalfeedback.text: Measuring stability takes ten minutes and assesses the property that actually decides whether a method can produce an apparatus.

answer.text: Because an apparatus that changes non-deterministically across executions cannot serve as a reliable, citeable foundation for scholarly debate.

feedback.text: Correct. Stability under identical premises is the essential prerequisite for critical scholarship; accuracy on a single lucky pass is insufficient.

answer.text: Because unstable models consume more electricity than deterministic Python scripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Power consumption is irrelevant to the epistemological stability of the edition.

answer.text: Because Moodle XML quizzes cannot import questions that have more than 80% accuracy.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Question banks can test any topic; stability is an editorial standard.

answer.text: Because stability measurements are required by the Greek Ministry of Culture.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stability is an internal criterion of scientific and editorial rigor.

questiontext.text: What characterizes a rigorous, scholarly conclusion regarding AI-assisted collation and classification?

generalfeedback.text: Report both the genuine advantage and the serious failure — a conclusion reporting only one of them is not a measurement.

answer.text: A balanced, quantified division of labour that reports both empirical capabilities (e.g. transposition detection) and specific failures (e.g. fabricated external claims).

feedback.text: Correct. Scholarly assessments avoid sweeping dismissals or uncritical hype, specifying exactly which subtasks are aided and which require strict human control.

answer.text: A blanket declaration that all human philologists will be replaced by neural networks within six months.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Uncritical hype ignores fundamental methodological limitations like external evidence and reproducibility.

answer.text: A total rejection of all computational tools in favor of 19th-century manual methods.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Total rejection ignores genuine efficiencies in classification and alignment.

answer.text: A single accuracy percentage without any breakdown by taxonomy tier or failure type.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Aggregated metrics hide crucial variations between easy and hard philological tasks.

questiontext.text: How do the three meetings of Topic 7 form a cohesive progression through the collation problem?

generalfeedback.text: Alignment is solved, definition is configuration, and classification needs semantics — three meetings, three distinct problems.

answer.text: Tuesday made tacit judgements visible; Wednesday solved mechanical sequence alignment via configuration; Friday tested semantic classification and exposed reproducibility limits.

feedback.text: Correct. The three steps demonstrate that alignment is solved computationally, definition is explicit configuration, and classification requires semantics with human oversight.

answer.text: Tuesday proved paper is obsolete; Wednesday proved Python is obsolete; Friday proved AI is obsolete.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Each method builds on the previous method's insights, establishing an integrated workflow.

answer.text: Tuesday focused on Latin; Wednesday focused on Syriac; Friday focused on Hebrew.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The entire week used the same Greek manuscript witnesses.

answer.text: The three meetings were unrelated introductory lectures with no unifying progression.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Topic 7 follows a structured three-step cycle (Manual, Deterministic, AI-assisted).

questiontext.text: Why does the epistemological burden of defining, classifying, and interpreting textual variance remain entirely with the human scholar?

generalfeedback.text: The tools produce the dataset; defining what counts, classifying it, and interpreting it remain the scholarship.

answer.text: Because algorithms and models only process sequence tokens or calculate probabilities; determining what counts as a variant and inferring transmission history are human scholarly acts.

feedback.text: Correct. Tools produce structured datasets, but textual criticism consists of defining research questions, applying taxonomy rules, and interpreting descent.

answer.text: Because digital editions are legally prohibited from citing software in academic bibliographies.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital tools are routinely cited in scholarly publications.

answer.text: Because computers refuse to process historical texts written prior to the invention of electricity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical texts from all periods are processed digitally.

answer.text: Because the TEI Consortium requires human signatures on every XML element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI encodes metadata and text; the intellectual responsibility rests with the editor.

questiontext.text: What are the three essential components that Week 8 will add to the collation dataset created in Topic 7?

generalfeedback.text: Week 8 adds the lemma, the significance filter, and the formal sigla — the three things this week's output deliberately lacks.

answer.text: The adopted lemma (), the significance filtering policy, and the formalized witness sigla declarations ().

feedback.text: Correct. Topic 7 produced the raw, classified variant record; Week 8 transforms that data into a formal critical apparatus.

answer.text: A full-color printed dust jacket, an ISBN number, and a retail barcode.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These are print distribution elements, not TEI apparatus components.

answer.text: Machine translation into five modern European languages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Critical apparatuses record manuscript readings in their authentic language.

answer.text: Automatic deletion of all minority manuscript readings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The apparatus criticus specifically records rejected minority readings inside elements.

questiontext.text: Why is tagging and pushing the repository state for the Normalization Assignment essential before leaving today's session?

generalfeedback.text: Tag and push the submitted state — three more weeks of work will otherwise make it unrecoverable.

answer.text: Subsequent work in Weeks 8 and 9 will modify the codebase, making it difficult to reconstruct the exact submitted state without a dedicated Git tag.

feedback.text: Correct. Tagging (e.g. submission-normalization) preserves an immutable snapshot of your submitted assignment in version control.

answer.text: Untagged commits are automatically erased from local storage after 24 hours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git retains commits, but tags provide explicit, human-readable milestones.

answer.text: The university registrar cancels student registration if Git tags are missing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tagging is an academic workflow practice, not an administrative penalty.

answer.text: Pushing tags converts XML files into read-only PDF documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tags are lightweight named pointers to specific commit hashes.

name.text: 22 Question: A Note on What Collation Cannot Settle

questiontext.text: When collating exactly two witnesses and finding two grammatical, sensible readings that explain each other equally well, how should the editor proceed?

generalfeedback.text: With two witnesses, many lemma choices cannot be settled by evidence — record them as judgements with the alternative preserved.

answer.text: Select a lemma on balance using internal criteria while recording the uncertainty with TEI @cert and preserving the alternative reading in the apparatus.

feedback.text: Correct. With two witnesses, ties cannot be broken by majority rule; scholarly honesty requires documenting editorial uncertainty rather than feigning confidence.

answer.text: Delete the sentence from the critical edition entirely to prevent reader confusion.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors do not censor text due to competing plausible readings.

answer.text: Declare that both scribes were illiterate and discard both manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Plausible variants reflect authentic historical transmission, not scribal illiteracy.

answer.text: Fabricate a third hypothetical witness to break the tie automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial apparatuses only record historical witnesses and conjectures explicitly marked as such.

name.text: 23 Question: Synthesis: Three Instruments, One Task

questiontext.text: How does understanding the distinct failure mode of each collation instrument guide the scholarly division of labour?

generalfeedback.text: Three instruments with three failure modes — random, systematic, and fabricating — and the division of labour follows from which failure you can afford where.

answer.text: Manual collation fails randomly via fatigue; automated alignment fails systematically via configuration; semantic models fail via fabrication and instability.

feedback.text: Correct. Knowing these failure modes dictates using deterministic alignment for the baseline, semantic models for classification assist, and human review for adjudication.

answer.text: All three instruments fail in the exact same way, so any instrument can be chosen at random.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Each instrument has a fundamentally distinct operational logic and risk profile.

answer.text: Manual collation has zero failure modes and should always replace computational tools.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual collation suffers severely from silent fatigue errors and cannot scale.

answer.text: Language models have zero failure modes when running on cloud GPUs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language models produce hallucinations and non-deterministic variations.

questiontext.text: Why has every single topic in this course begun with a manual, hand-crafted reference step before introducing computational automation?

generalfeedback.text: Every week produced a hand-made reference because an automated method cannot be evaluated against its own output.

answer.text: Because automated methods cannot be evaluated against their own output; an independent, hand-crafted ground truth is required to assess tool performance.

feedback.text: Correct. Without a manual reference, systematic machine errors remain invisible and unmeasurable.

answer.text: Because digital tools are unreliable and should never be used in actual scholarship.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital tools are central to the course; manual baselines allow rigorous evaluation of them.

answer.text: Because the university lacks sufficient electrical power to run computers on Tuesdays.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The pedagogical structure is methodological and scientific, not infrastructure-related.

answer.text: Because hand-written paper notes are required by Canadian copyright law.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual baselines provide empirical ground truth for benchmarking.

questiontext.text: What is the strategic purpose of Week 10 ('Consolidation') in the second half of the course curriculum?

generalfeedback.text: Week 10 is deliberate slack with no new method — work that slips in Weeks 8 and 9 has somewhere to land.

answer.text: It provides deliberate slack with no new methods introduced, allowing students to reconcile accumulated layers, address gaps, and refine their editions.

feedback.text: Correct. Complex multi-layered digital editions require scheduled integration time to ensure all transcription, normalization, and apparatus layers align.

answer.text: It is an official campus holiday where no course work is permitted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Week 10 is an active instructional week dedicated to project consolidation.

answer.text: It replaces all TEI XML files with plain text Markdown documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML remains the central archival encoding standard throughout the course.

answer.text: It requires students to learn an entirely new programming language from scratch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Week 10 introduces no new methods, focusing on reconciling existing layers.

name.text: 26 Question: A Note on Accumulated Documentation

questiontext.text: What role do the accumulated method files (METHOD.md, ORTHOGRAPHY.md, CONVENTIONS.md) play in the final critical edition?

generalfeedback.text: The accumulated method documents are the edition's front matter and the source of its commentary — the recording is the scholarship, not overhead on it.

answer.text: They form the comprehensive, searchable editorial front matter and provide the evidential basis for the textual commentary in Week 12.

feedback.text: Correct. Digital documentation makes every editorial premise, decision rule, and normalization explicit, allowing readers to assess the edition's arguments.

answer.text: They are private developer logs that must be deleted prior to publication in Week 13.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transparent documentation is a permanent, vital component of the published edition.

answer.text: They are compiled into binary DLL files to speed up web browser rendering.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Method files are scholarly markdown texts intended for human readers and evaluators.

answer.text: They serve as legal disclaimers protecting the university from copyright lawsuits.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Method documents explain editorial choices and philological policies.

questiontext.text: How does the economic trade-off between manual collation and automated pipelines behave as corpus scale increases?

generalfeedback.text: Configuration cost is fixed and automation's value scales with the work — say honestly which side of that threshold your passage falls on.

answer.text: Manual collation has zero setup cost but high marginal cost per line; automated pipelines have a fixed upfront configuration cost but negligible marginal cost at scale.

feedback.text: Correct. On short passages manual collation is competitive; on traditions of hundreds of witnesses or millions of words, automation is the only viable option.

answer.text: Manual collation becomes cheaper as corpus size increases due to human reading speed acceleration.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human fatigue increases and error rates rise as corpus size grows.

answer.text: Automated collation costs increase exponentially with every additional word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Once configured, alignment algorithms process massive token lists in seconds.

answer.text: Cloud computing costs make automated collation impossible for universities.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX runs locally on standard consumer computers with negligible cost.

name.text: 28 Question: Reproducibility as an Editorial Value

questiontext.text: Why is distinguishing between re-derivable claims and claims resting on editorial authority essential in a digital critical edition?

generalfeedback.text: Some claims can be re-derived and some rest on the editor's authority — what matters is that the edition says which are which.

answer.text: It informs the reader which textual claims can be verified algorithmically from stated premises and which require trusting the scholar's qualitative judgement.

feedback.text: Correct. Transparency about what is computational and what is interpretive allows readers to evaluate the edition's conclusions with appropriate rigor.

answer.text: Re-derivable claims are protected by patents, while editorial claims are public domain.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly editions do not patent editorial claims; the distinction is epistemological.

answer.text: Claims resting on authority are automatically deleted during TEI schema validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI accommodates both authority declarations (@resp) and rule-based markup.

answer.text: Digital editions must contain zero qualitative judgements to be accepted by libraries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Critical scholarship is inherently interpretive; digital methods make those judgements explicit.

questiontext.text: Why must students verify that all local Git commits and tags have been pushed to the remote repository at the end of Topic 7?

generalfeedback.text: Confirm tags reached the remote — an unpushed week is a week at risk.

answer.text: Unpushed commits and tags remain only on the local machine and risk permanent data loss or loss of synchronization across work sessions.

feedback.text: Correct. Confirming that tags reached the remote remote ensures that your evaluated milestone is safely backed up and accessible.

answer.text: Remote servers automatically delete repositories that do not receive hourly push notifications.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Remote repositories are persistent, but unpushed local changes are vulnerable to hardware failure.

answer.text: Pushing tags converts the repository into a read-only Wikipedia page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git remotes host version-controlled code, not static Wikipedia articles.

answer.text: The course instructor cannot assign midterm grades without an active SSH connection.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pushing code to GitHub/GitLab makes your work verifiable for grading.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: The Dataset and the Criticism

questiontext.text: What is the ultimate distinction between automated collation datasets and textual criticism as established by Topic 7?

generalfeedback.text: This week produced the evidence; Week 8 begins the inference, one editorial decision at a time.

answer.text: Automated tools assemble a structured dataset of aligned textual variance; textual criticism is the scholarly act of interpreting that evidence and establishing the text.

feedback.text: Correct. Algorithms do not do the criticism; they provide the mathematically sound foundation upon which human editorial judgements are made.

answer.text: Automated collation datasets are critical editions in their finished form.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Raw collation data lacks lemma selection, apparatus filtering, and commentary.

answer.text: Textual criticism is obsolete now that dynamic programming algorithms exist.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Algorithms only process tokens; evaluating transmission and meaning remains essential.

answer.text: Collation datasets are created purely for computational linguists and have no value for editors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collation datasets are the indispensable evidence base for critical editing.
